blocks.text: Benzene, C6H6, is one of the most important organic compounds and the simplest aromatic hydrocarbon. Many compounds derived from benzene have pleasant smells, so in the early 19th century compounds containing benzene rings were called aromatic (sweet-smelling); vanilla is an example. Hydrocarbons containing one or more benzene rings are called arenes. Today the word aromatic is used for molecules with benzene or benzene-like rings, whatever their smell; some smell unpleasant.

blocks.title: Did you know?
blocks.text: Not every good-smelling compound is aromatic. Camphor, from the camphor laurel tree, has a strong minty smell but no benzene ring in its structure.

Once the molecular formula C6H6 was known, chemists proposed several linear structures, but these could not explain benzene's properties. In 1865 the German professor August Kekule proposed a six-membered ring with alternating single and double bonds. This explained many properties, but not all of its physical and chemical behaviour.

blocks.alt: Left: Kekule's benzene, a hexagon of six C atoms with alternating single and double bonds and an H on each carbon, beside the modern hexagon-with-circle symbol. Right: the X-ray picture, a regular flat hexagon with a circle, C-C bonds of 139 pm, C-H bonds of 109 pm and 120 degree angles.
blocks.caption: Kekule's structure and the measured shape of benzene (original diagram after the book's structures).
blocks.long_description: X-ray studies show that benzene is planar: a regular hexagon of six sp2 carbon atoms. Each carbon is joined to three other atoms with bond angles of 120 degrees for C-C-C and H-C-C. The C-H bond is 109 pm long and every C-C bond is 139 pm, between the C-C single bond (154 pm) and the C=C double bond (133 pm). Kekule's alternating single and double bonds would give two different bond lengths.
